name: Interview finance, set 1
description: Finance questions of the kind asked in first rounds: rates, bonds, forwards, dividends, parity, spreads, Greeks, trees, order books, costs and value at risk. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: A deposit pays 6% a year, compounded monthly.
items.question: What is the effective annual rate, in per cent to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow £1 at the monthly rate for twelve months.

byKey.continuous: You compounded continuously, $e^{0.06} - 1$. Monthly compounding adds slightly less.
byKey.nominal: You gave the quoted rate. Interest paid each month earns interest in later months.

explain.text: The monthly rate is $6\%/12 = 0.5\%$. Over a year £1 grows to $1.005^{12} \approx 1.0617$. So the effective rate is about 6.17%.

items.prose: A bond has modified duration 7. Its yield rises by 25 basis points.
items.question: What is the approximate change in its price, in per cent to 2 decimal places? Use a minus sign for a fall.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the duration by the yield change in decimal form.

byKey.sign: You gave a rise. Prices fall when yields rise, so the change is negative.
byKey.basis-points: You read 25 basis points as 2.5%. A basis point is 0.01%, so 25 of them are 0.25%.

explain.text: Modified duration gives the price change as $-D \times \Delta y$. Here that is $-7 \times 0.0025 = -0.0175$. The price falls by about 1.75%.

items.prose: A share trades at £80 and pays no dividends. The interest rate is 5% a year, continuously compounded.
items.question: What is the fair six-month forward price, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow the share price at the continuous rate for half a year.

byKey.simple: You used simple interest, 80 times 1.025. The rate is continuously compounded, so use $e^{0.025}$.
byKey.full-year: You grew the price for a full year. The forward is for six months, so the exponent is 0.025.

explain.text: Buying the share now and holding it costs the price plus the interest forgone. So the forward is $80e^{0.05 \times 0.5} = 80e^{0.025}$. That is about £82.03.

items.prose: A share will pay a dividend of £3 next year. The dividend grows 4% a year for ever. Investors want a return of 9% a year.
items.question: What is the share worth today, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the growing stream of dividends at the required return.

byKey.no-growth: You divided by 0.09 alone. Growth of 4% a year lowers the effective discount to 5%.
byKey.grew-again: You grew the first dividend by 4% again. The £3 is already next year's payment.

explain.text: A dividend growing at g for ever, discounted at r, is worth $D_1/(r - g)$. Here that is $3/(0.09 - 0.04)$. That is $3/0.05 = 60$ pounds.

items.prose: A share at £80 pays no dividends. Its European call, struck at £84 with three months to run, is priced at £4.10. Interest is 6% a year with continuous compounding.
items.question: What is the matching European put worth, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: £6.85: 4.10 less 80 plus 84 times e to the power -0.015.
widget.label: Put price in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write put-call parity and solve it for the put.

byKey.undiscounted: You used the strike of £84 undiscounted. The strike is paid in three months, so it is worth $84e^{-0.015}$ today.
byKey.signs-swapped: You swapped the share and the discounted strike. The put equals the call less the share plus the discounted strike.

explain.text: Put-call parity says $C - P = S - Ke^{-rT}$. Here $Ke^{-rT} = 84e^{-0.015} \approx 82.75$. So $P = 4.10 - 80 + 82.75 = 6.85$ pounds.

items.prose: On one share and expiry, you buy the 40-strike call for £7. You also sell the 50-strike call for £3.
items.question: At what share price at expiry do you break even, in pounds?

widget.accept: £44: the lower strike plus the net cost of £4.
widget.label: Break-even in pounds

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the net cost, then ask where the long call earns it back.

byKey.one-premium: You ignored the £3 you received. The spread costs £7 less £3, which is £4.
byKey.both-premiums: You added both premiums. You paid £7 and received £3, so the net cost is £4.

explain.text: The spread costs $7 - 3 = 4$ pounds. Below 50 only the 40 call pays, and it earns back £4 when the share is at 44. So the break-even price is £44.

items.prose: A call costs £4.00, with delta 0.45 and gamma 0.05. The share then rises by £2.
items.question: Using delta and gamma, what is the call's estimated new price, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the delta term and half of gamma times the move squared.

byKey.delta-only: You kept the delta term only. Gamma adds $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.05 \times 2^2 = 0.10$.
byKey.no-half: You left out the half on the gamma term. The second-order term is half of gamma times the move squared.
byKey.change-only: You gave the change in price. Add it to the £4.00 the call cost.

explain.text: The change is about $\Delta\,dS + \tfrac{1}{2}\Gamma\,dS^2$. Here that is $0.45 \times 2 + 0.5 \times 0.05 \times 4 = 1$. So the call is worth about £5.00.

items.prose: A share at 100 will move to 120 or to 90 in one step. Money grows by 5% over the step.
items.question: What is a call struck at 105 worth today, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the up probability that makes the share earn the rate, then discount.

byKey.undiscounted: You took the expected payoff, 7.50, and stopped. It is paid at the end of the step, so divide by 1.05.
byKey.zero-rate: You found the up probability as if the rate were zero, 1/3. With 5% growth it is 0.5.

explain.text: The risk-neutral up probability solves $120q + 90(1 - q) = 105$, so $q = 0.5$. The call pays 15 after a rise and 0 after a fall. Its value is $0.5 \times 15/1.05 \approx 7.14$.

items.prose: A share starts at 100. Each step it rises 10% or falls 10%, and money grows 5% a step. There are two steps.
items.question: What is an American put struck at 100 worth today, to 2 decimal places?

widget.accept: 2.55: exercise after the first fall, worth 10 there.
widget.label: Put value

feedback.generic: Not quite right. At each node, take the larger of exercising now and the discounted value of waiting.

byKey.european: You valued the European put. After the first fall the share is at 90, and exercising for 10 beats waiting.
byKey.root-undiscounted: You did not discount the last step back to today. Divide the root's expected value by 1.05.

explain.text: The up probability is $q = (1.05 - 0.9)/0.2 = 0.75$, and the put pays 0, 1 or 19 at the end. At 90, waiting is worth $(0.75 + 0.25 \times 19)/1.05 \approx 5.24$, so you exercise for 10; at 110 it is worth about 0.238. The root is $(0.75 \times 0.238 + 0.25 \times 10)/1.05 \approx 2.55$.

items.prose: The offers in a book are 100 shares at £10.01, 200 at £10.02 and 500 at £10.04. A market order buys 400 shares.
items.question: What is the average price paid, in pounds to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill level by level, then divide the total cost by 400.

byKey.unweighted: You averaged the three prices equally. Weight each by the shares bought there: 100, 200 and 100.
byKey.last-price: You gave the last price touched. The order paid less on its first 300 shares.

explain.text: The order takes 100 at 10.01, 200 at 10.02 and 100 at 10.04. That costs $1001 + 2004 + 1004 = 4009$ pounds. The average is $4009/400 = 10.0225$.

items.prose: The bid is £19.98 and the ask is £20.02. Your buy order fills at £20.01.
items.question: What is the effective spread, in basis points of the mid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure your fill against the mid, then double it.

byKey.quoted: You gave the quoted spread, 0.04 over 20. The effective spread uses your fill against the mid.
byKey.not-doubled: You stopped at the half-spread. The effective spread doubles the distance from the mid.

explain.text: The mid is £20.00, and your fill sits £0.01 above it. The effective spread is twice that distance over the mid, $0.02/20 = 0.001$. That is 10 basis points.

items.prose: You hold shares with a sell stop at £95. A colleague holds the same shares with a stop-limit to sell, stop and limit both at £95. Bad news arrives, and the next trade prints at £93. Each order wakes once a trade prints at or below its stop price.
items.question: What happens to the two orders?

options.text: The stop sells near £93; the stop-limit rests unfilled at £95.
Both orders sell at £95, the price each of them named.
options.why: You treated the stop price as a promised fill. Once triggered, a stop is a market order and takes the next price.

options.text: Both orders sell near £93, the first price after the gap.
options.why: You treated the stop-limit as a plain stop. It becomes a limit order at £95 and cannot sell below that.

options.text: Neither order triggers, as no trade printed at £95.
options.why: You waited for a trade at exactly £95. A sell stop triggers on a trade at or below its price.

feedback.correct: Correct. The stop fills near £93; the stop-limit waits.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each order becomes once a trade prints at or below £95.

explain.text: Once a trade prints at or below £95, a sell stop becomes a market order and sells near £93. The stop-limit becomes a limit order to sell at £95 or better. With the market at £93 no buyer meets it, so it rests unfilled.

items.prose: You buy a one-month at-the-money call and sell a six-month call at the same strike, on the same share. The interest rate is zero.
items.question: Which signs does the spread have for gamma, vega and theta?

options.text: Positive gamma, negative vega, negative theta
Negative gamma, positive vega, positive theta
options.why: You reversed which leg is larger for each Greek. Short-dated options carry more gamma and theta; long-dated ones carry more vega.

options.text: Negative gamma, negative vega, positive theta
options.why: You took the signs of the short six-month call alone. The one-month call has the larger gamma and theta, so net gamma is positive and net theta negative.

options.text: Positive gamma, positive vega, negative theta
options.why: You took the signs of the long one-month call alone. The short six-month call has the larger vega, so net vega is negative.

feedback.correct: Correct. Long gamma, short vega, paying theta.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which expiry carries more of each Greek at the money.

explain.text: Near expiry, an at-the-money option has more gamma and theta but less vega. So the long one-month call sets the sign of gamma and theta, and the six-month call sets vega. At spot 100 and vol 20%, the net gamma is +0.0409, vega -16.63 and theta -8.19 a year.

items.prose: You hold a £3,000,000 position. Its daily returns are normal with mean zero and volatility 1.2%. Use 2.326 for the 99% point of the normal.
items.question: What is the one-day 99% value at risk, to the nearest pound?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the position, the daily volatility and the 99% point.

byKey.used-1-645: You used 1.645, the 95% point. A 99% value at risk uses 2.326.
byKey.ten-day: You scaled to ten days by the root of 10. The question asks for one day.
byKey.one-sd: You stopped at one standard deviation of the day's loss. The 99% point is 2.326 of those.

explain.text: The one-day loss has standard deviation $3{,}000{,}000 \times 0.012 = 36{,}000$ pounds. The 99% value at risk is 2.326 of those. That is $2.326 \times 36{,}000 = 83{,}736$ pounds.

items.prose: A share trades at £150 with volatility 32% a year. A call is at the money and expires in one sixteenth of a year. The interest rate is zero.
items.question: By the 0.4 rule of thumb, what is the call worth, in pounds to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The rule is 0.4 times the share price times the volatility times the root of the time.

byKey.no-root: You used the time, 1/16, in place of its root, 1/4.
byKey.no-time: You left out the time factor. Multiply by the root of 1/16, which is 0.25.

explain.text: An at-the-money call is worth about $0.4\,S\sigma\sqrt{T}$, since $1/\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 0.4$. Here $\sqrt{1/16} = 0.25$, so the call is about $0.4 \times 150 \times 0.32 \times 0.25 = 4.8$ pounds. The full Black-Scholes value is £4.79.
